name: Járngreipr
powers: Let Thor grip the white-hot shaft of Mjölnir.
description: The iron gauntlets of Thor, one of his three great treasures named in the Prose Edda. Their purpose is practical as much as martial: the handle of Mjölnir grows white-hot in flight, and only the iron gloves allow Thor to grasp the hammer and throw it. The third treasure completes the set — the strength belt Megingjörð.

name: Yule Goat
description: The Yule goat (julbock), a goat figure of straw bound with red ribbon, made in Sweden at Christmas. The straw goat descends from older beliefs around Thor's goats and the 'julbock' who once brought the Christmas gifts before the tree took the role. Today the most famous example is the giant Gävle goat, erected and burned each December.
source: Swedish Christmas tradition of the julbock

name: The Jelling Stones
powers: King Harald's runes proclaim that he won Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.
description: The two great runestones of the royal monument at Jelling, Jutland, raised by kings Gorm and Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. Harald's stone, carved with the oldest portrait of Christ in Denmark, announces that he 'won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian', marking Denmark's conversion. The stones stand in the churchyard as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

name: Jade Dragon
powers: Symbol of imperial authority and protection; believed to ward off evil spirits.
description: A finely carved jade dragon pendant used by nobles during the Han Dynasty. The dragon motif represented celestial power and was worn as a talisman to ensure the bearer's prestige and safety.

name: The Singing Harp
powers: Sang on its own and cried out for its master, waking the giant.
description: The singing golden harp of the giant in the tale of Jack and the Beanstalk. As Jack climbs down the beanstalk with the hen and the gold, the harp calls out for its master, waking the giant and setting the chase in motion. It is one of the three treasures the giant keeps in his castle.
source: Jack and the Beanstalk (English fairy tale)

name: The Jambiya
powers: Symbol of honor and manhood; drawn in the bara' dance.
description: The short curved dagger with a broad double-edged blade worn at the belt by Yemeni men, a symbol of honor and manhood carried from youth and drawn in the bara' war dance. Silver-sheathed jambiya hilts, some of rhino horn, are treasured heirlooms and marks of tribal standing. The weapon is attested across Yemeni material culture and in the dances, songs, and poetry that surround it.
source: Yemeni material culture and ethnographic records

name: Jiu Ding
powers: Signifies the Mandate of Heaven and legitimacy of rule
description: The nine bronze tripods (jiu ding) that culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces, inscribing each region's creatures so the people could recognize them. Passed between the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality on the moon, a familiar figure in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery. The rabbit is said to grind herbs under the cassia tree for Chang'e, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore, including Korean tales of a rabbit on the lunar surface.
source: Han bronze mirrors and moon-rabbit tradition

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
powers: Summoned rain when struck by the frog
description: In a Vietnamese folk tale, a frog led a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never fell, then beat the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong until the god sent rain. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta.
